title: System Time Discovery
summary: System time discovery is the reading of a host clock, time zone or uptime, either locally or across the network. Accurate time is rarely the objective by itself: it lets an adversary schedule a task for a quiet hour, align beacon sleep intervals, timestamp staged files, or judge whether a sandbox has been running long enough to look like a real workstation. On Windows the classic forms are net time against a remote host name and w32tm /tz for the local time zone, while macOS and Linux expose the same information through tools such as systemsetup, timedatectl and clock system files. Network devices and hypervisors answer comparable queries, for example show clock detail on a switch or an esxcli clock query on an ESXi host. Because authentication, patching and monitoring generate constant time traffic, detection has to key on unusual sources or targets, on direct clock queries from interactive shells, or on a clock query appearing in the same short sequence as other discovery commands.

beginner.definition: System time discovery means an attacker reads the clock, the time zone or the uptime of a computer. Uptime is how long the computer has been switched on. This information helps them plan when to act and check what kind of system they are on.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many attacker actions depend on time, such as running a job at three in the morning when nobody is watching. Reading the clock also helps them test for an analysis system, because such systems often report a short uptime. The activity itself looks harmless and is very common, so it rarely raises an alarm on its own. It matters because it often comes just before something serious.
howItWorks: The attacker runs a command or script on a host, or points one at another host.
On Windows, net time against a host name reads that machine's clock, and w32tm /tz shows the local time zone.
On macOS and Linux, tools such as systemsetup or timedatectl return the same details.
Network devices and virtual hosts answer similar queries about their own clocks.
The attacker also checks uptime, to guess whether the system is a real machine or a test environment.
The results feed later steps, such as scheduling a task or setting the sleep time between connections.
beginner.example: A new night porter in a hotel walks the corridors and notes every clock. That includes the lobby clock and the one in the kitchen. The clocks do not open any doors. But knowing them tells the porter exactly when the corridors are empty and when the deliveries arrive. That is why nobody watches the porter writing down times.
takeaways: Time queries look harmless and are everywhere, so context matters more than the action.
Uptime checks are a common sign that malware is testing for an analysis environment.
Time discovery often appears next to other discovery commands in the same short window.

objectives: Explain what system time, time zone and uptime mean to an attacker.
Describe the Windows commands used to read time locally and on a remote host.
Explain why time discovery supports task scheduling and connection timing.
Describe how uptime is used to detect analysis environments.
Explain why clock queries are difficult to detect on their own.
